source_terms: It is usually assumed that marketers use scientific methods to determine the price of their products. Nothing could be further from the truth. In almost every case, the process of decision is one of guesswork.
The higher you price your product, the more desirable it becomes in the eyes of the consumer.

Yet when Professor Reisz of the University of Iowa tried to relate the prices of 679 brands of food products to their quality , he found that the correlation between quality and price was almost zero.
item.claim: The source sets three statements about price beside one another without smoothing the tension. Pricing is not scientific: in almost every case the decision is guesswork. The higher the price, the more desirable the product becomes in the consumer's eyes. And a study relating the prices of six hundred and seventy-nine food brands to their quality found the correlation almost zero. He reports marketers being afraid to price above competition, quotes a research director who said his company had never gone to market with the best product he could make because marketers forced an inferior product at a lower price, and says there were signs of a trend towards superior products at premium prices.

scope.conditions: consumer packaged goods, and food products in the cited study

caveats.text: the two claims are compatible and the compatibility is the interesting part: price is read by buyers as evidence of quality while carrying almost no information about it. The source states both and does not draw that conclusion
the research chapter separately reports the same signal working in a controlled setting, with identical cheeses at two prices and the dearer selling faster

the study is named with its author, institution and sample size and its result is given, which makes it one of the better-documented citations in the book; the quality measure it used is not described
the closing line of the passage — that the consumer is not a moron, she is your wife — is the source's own, quoting himself from an earlier era, and carries the address of his period

source_stated_problems: the process of decision is one of guesswork

intra_source_relations.note: the survey finding that consumers judge quality by price, tested against measured quality
the source states pricing as one of the two questions research cannot answer

provenance.chapter: 16 — What little I know about marketing

item.rationale: SPEC-01 names a typography_layout field and does not say what may go in it. This source supplies a complete and closed vocabulary for it: columns and their gutters, flowlines, rows and their gutters, modules, spatial zones and markers, with the source's own statement that every grid is made of these and no others. A layout specified in these terms is machine-comparable in the way SPEC-01 wants element references to be.

applicability.when: specifying or reading the layout structure of a static piece
applicability.limits: The vocabulary is for orthogonal, alignment-based structures. The source's own hierarchic grid is defined by intuitive placement, and a layout with no repeating interval can be described in these terms only loosely.

source_terms: To build a quality brand you need to narrow the focus and combine that narrow focus with a better name and a higher price.
What can we put into our brand to justify the higher price?
item.claim: The authors' constructive prescription for quality perception has three components, and they state that the way to build it is to follow the other laws rather than to improve the product. Narrowing makes a brand a specialist, and specialists are perceived to know more; a better name beats an equal competitor with a worse one; a high price is itself a benefit, because it lets a buyer take public satisfaction from consumption. They invert the conventional order of design: instead of building quality and pricing to match, start with a higher price and then ask what can be put into the brand to justify it.

mechanism.text: Specialist perception is argued from the cardiologist against the general practitioner — most people believe the specialist knows more, and the authors say from a marketing point of view it does not matter whether that is true. High price works socially rather than functionally: the Rolex wearer is not buying punctuality but the public fact of affordability, and the authors ask whether $100 jeans would sell at that price with the label inside.

scope.conditions: the price move is offered specifically for 'a sea of similar products with similar prices'

caveats.text: the authors qualify their own advice: they say they always advise clients to build as much quality as they can afford, so this is a claim about what builds the brand, not a licence to build a worse product

the justification examples (a bigger and heavier watch, an oversized driver, a fatter pen, more butterfat, longer ageing) are product changes chosen after the brands succeeded; no case is given of the same tactic failing

source_stated_problems: conventional wisdom often advocates marketing a high-quality product at a comparable price
source_stated_remedies: deliberately start with a higher price

positive.description: brands the authors say benefit from high price, and the specific product changes used to justify the price in five of them

intra_source_relations.note: supplies the constructive half of the Law of Quality
narrow focus is one of the three components

results.caution: HOLD: unresolved evidence or representation blocker. Not accepted Canon.

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

INSPECTED: Figure 4.2, the premium-popular-discount construct, was opened. It is a schematic price-against-performance diagram showing the traditional line and three 'new offering' positions below it; it carries no data and is an illustration of the argument, not evidence for it

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: Named cases without figures; a competing explanation for the same phenomenon appears elsewhere in the book unreconciled.

source_stated_problems: a shift in observed behaviour caused by a moving choice set is attributed to consumer character
source_stated_remedies: check whether the price-performance frontier moved before attributing a behaviour change to the buyer

positive: TVS Victor, a 125cc motorcycle offered at a 100cc popular price
Maruti Swift, a 'B' segment car with premium-category features

intra_source_relations.note: the segmentation being invalidated [relation re-expressed from the non-SPEC-03 'supported_by' by semantic review of this note]

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Intuitive, Relational, and Conceptual: 'Imagery as a Source' (spine 6)
item.question: Samara asks what happens if the imagery is allowed to rule a layout. What reason does he give for expecting that inversion to be productive, and what are the two directions it can take?
item.answer: His reason is an asymmetry of vocabulary: typography is always a pattern of lines, whereas images present a radically greater range of form languages. Applying an image's language to text therefore relieves the designer quickly of presumptions about how text should behave in a layout, or how layouts ought to be organised — presumptions he says are hard to dislodge because type and image are usually assumed to be mutually dominant and referential. The two directions are: one in which typographic elements become, in essence, part of the imagery; and one in which the imagery sets up the logic for how type responds to it pictorially, while the type retains its identity as a separate entity alongside the images.
item.support: "Imagery as a Source": type and image notoriously challenging to combine; typography always a pattern of lines against images' greater range of form languages; the two named directions.
confounders: reading it as advice to make type look like a picture in general
assuming the type must always merge into the image — he names a second direction in which it stays separate
assuming the correspondence must be literal; elsewhere he says the mere fact of a shared quality is enough
